iut_type: RF 2-item confirmatory test requirement for an antenna-fed-via-PCB-trace surface-mount module, even when using a certified Host Subsystem stack -- pass rate and host-OS irrelevance for RF-only testing
customer_question: If we use a Controller Subsystem QDID combined with a properly certified, purchased Host Subsystem stack, can registration proceed via paperwork alone (final product registration only), or are L2CAP/GAP/SPP-type protocol tests still required? And does our Linux-based (non-Android) system require different testing?
question_variants: Does a surface-mount module's antenna feed method ever require RF testing even when the Host Stack itself is already certified?
Does the choice of host operating system (Linux vs. Android) affect RF PHY test requirements?
actual_issue: The customer assumed that combining an existing certified Controller Subsystem QDID with a properly licensed, certified Host Subsystem stack would allow registration via documentation alone, with no testing required, and separately wanted to know whether their Linux-based (rather than Android-based) system introduced any testing differences.
plain_english_explanation: Implementing a properly certified Host Subsystem stack does eliminate the need for protocol/profile-layer testing (L2CAP, GAP, SPP, etc.) -- that part of the customer's assumption was correct. However, a separate testing requirement can still apply based on the physical module's antenna feed design: in this case, the specific module type was a surface-mount module where the antenna signal is fed via the product board's PCB trace pattern to the antenna, rather than through a fixed, pre-validated antenna connection. This physical configuration requires an RF 2-item test (transmit power, receive sensitivity) -- performed by extracting the antenna signal near its feed point -- specifically to confirm that the product board's PCB trace pattern design doesn't degrade RF performance. This RF 2-item test has historically had a 98% pass rate, and is conducted at Allion's Japan lab using a modified RF test sample and a simple DUT-mode-entry procedure document, with no need for the customer's engineer to be physically present for the test. Separately, regarding the host OS question: since the RF 2-item test only exercises the HCI layer and below (i.e., the low-level radio/controller functionality), the choice of host-layer operating system (Linux, Android, or anything else) makes no difference to this specific test -- the OS only matters for protocol/profile-layer testing, which isn't required here since a certified Host stack is being used.
consultant_answer: You're right that protocol/profile testing (L2CAP, GAP, SPP, etc.) isn't needed once you implement a certified Host Subsystem stack. However, since your specific module is a surface-mount type where the antenna signal is fed via the product board's PCB trace pattern, you'll still need an RF 2-item test (transmit power, receive sensitivity) to confirm the board pattern design doesn't degrade performance -- this has a 98% historical pass rate and doesn't require your presence, just a modified RF test sample and a simple DUT-mode procedure document sent to our Japan lab. And no, since this RF test only exercises the HCI layer and below, your Linux-based host OS makes no difference -- the OS choice only matters for protocol/profile testing, which you don't need here.
decision_logic: When a customer implements a certified Host Subsystem stack and assumes no testing is needed, check the underlying module's antenna feed design -- a surface-mount module with PCB-trace-routed antenna feed still requires an RF 2-item confirmatory test regardless of Host Stack certification status, while protocol/profile testing is genuinely unnecessary in that scenario; and clarify that RF-only testing is host-OS-agnostic since it only exercises HCI-layer-and-below functionality.
final_recommendation: When scoping testing requirements for a product using a certified Host Subsystem stack, proactively check the physical module's antenna feed configuration (fixed connection vs. PCB-trace-routed) rather than assuming certified-stack implementation eliminates all testing, and reassure customers with non-Android host OSes that RF-only testing is unaffected by their OS choice.
risk_if_done_wrong: Assuming a certified Host Subsystem stack eliminates all testing requirements could result in an incomplete registration if the module's antenna feed design actually requires the RF 2-item confirmatory test.
